At the edge of the city, where the last bus sighs and turns around, there’s a little patch of grass that refuses to become anything else.

In spring, it grows crooked daisies. In summer, it hosts a stubborn dandelion that outlasts every lawn mower. By October, the grass turns the color of old postcards, and fallen leaves gather there as if they’ve made plans.

People pass it without looking. They’re carrying groceries, rehearsing conversations, thinking about bills or dinner or the strange message they haven’t answered. The patch asks nothing of them. It doesn’t mind being overlooked. It simply keeps being a patch of grass.

I think there’s comfort in that—not that everything has a secret meaning, or that the world is quietly arranging itself around us, but that so much of it continues without needing our attention. A tree puts on leaves. Rain finds the cracks in the pavement. Somewhere, an ordinary flower opens in a place no one meant to plant one.

And if you happen to notice, even for a second, the day becomes a little wider.
